title: B-tree Equality
summary: Use a btree index for exact lookup, foreign-key joins, and ordered scans on scalar columns. This is the default index pattern for stable relational predicates.
tradeoffs: Excellent default for equality and ordering, but not a fix for low-selectivity predicates.

title: Composite Equality Then Range
summary: Put equality columns first and the range or ordering column after them. Reach for this when tenant, status, or account filters narrow the rows before time or amount ranges.
tradeoffs: Column order is workload-specific and can become redundant with nearby indexes.

title: Covering B-tree With INCLUDE
summary: Use INCLUDE columns when a hot query can be served from an index without widening the search key. It fits read paths where a few projected columns dominate latency.
tradeoffs: Covering indexes reduce heap visits but add write cost and can duplicate other indexes.

title: Partial Index for Skew
summary: Index only active, pending, recent, or otherwise skewed rows when hot queries use that predicate. This keeps high-value indexes small and cheaper to maintain.
tradeoffs: The query predicate must match the index predicate closely or the planner cannot use it.

title: Expression Index for Normalization
summary: Index deterministic expressions such as lower(email) or extracted JSONB keys when queries use the same expression. Reach for this when normalization belongs near the data.
tradeoffs: Expression drift between application code and SQL can silently miss the index.

title: GIN JSONB Containment
summary: Use GIN when JSONB containment predicates are a proven hot path. It is best for selective document-key queries that remain valid JSONB use cases.
tradeoffs: GIN indexes are write-heavy and do not rescue facts that should be typed columns.

title: GIN Trigram Similarity
summary: Use trigram GIN indexes for fuzzy names, titles, support search, and substring matching. Reach for it after exact lookup and full-text search have been separated from typo tolerance.
tradeoffs: Large text columns and frequent writes can make trigram indexes expensive.

title: GIN Array Membership
summary: Use GIN for containment and membership checks on small bounded arrays. It fits tags and flags, not arrays pretending to be child tables.
tradeoffs: Element-level lifecycle or joins should move the model to relational child rows.

title: GiST Range Exclusion
summary: Use GiST with range operators and exclusion constraints to prevent overlaps. This is the natural pattern for booking, availability, and validity-window correctness.
tradeoffs: Concurrent write behavior must be tested because the index enforces business conflicts.

title: GiST Geospatial
summary: Use GiST for PostGIS geometry and geography predicates such as intersects, contains, and distance prefilters. Reach for it when spatial predicates are part of the workload.
tradeoffs: Spatial indexes need coordinate-system discipline and query shapes that expose spatial operators.

title: BRIN for Append-only Time
summary: Use BRIN on large append-only chronological tables where physical order correlates with time. It is compact and effective for recent-window or range scans.
tradeoffs: BRIN is approximate and weak when rows are not physically correlated with the indexed value.

title: HNSW Vector ANN
summary: Use HNSW for pgvector approximate nearest-neighbor search when recall and latency requirements justify memory-heavy indexes. It fits serving paths that need strong interactive retrieval.
tradeoffs: HNSW can be memory-intensive and must be tested with tenant and permission filters.

title: IVFFlat Vector ANN
summary: Use IVFFlat for pgvector approximate nearest-neighbor search when training and list tuning are acceptable. It can be cheaper than HNSW for some bulk workloads.
tradeoffs: Recall depends on list and probe tuning, and indexes should be rebuilt after major data distribution changes.
